responses.answer:
Use one persistent assistant with a scheduling policy you approve once and a permission check before every send. Reading your calendar and inbox, and being technically able to send email, does not authorize every scheduling decision. The supplied capabilities also do not include editing your calendar.

Watch only the calendar and inbox you designate. Use change notifications where available, with a proposed five-minute reconciliation check. Deduplicate repeated notifications and recheck current availability before proposing or confirming a time.

| Verdict | Condition and response |
|---|---|
| **Act** | Read requests, compare availability and prepare drafts. Send only an exact message you already approved, or a message covered by an active scheduling grant. |
| **Ask** | Conflicting commitments, ambiguous dates or time zones, a first-ever correspondent, an expired or unmatched grant, or any condition absent from the rules. Present one question with concrete options, a recommended choice and a reply deadline. |
| **Hand off** | Authentication codes, password or recovery changes, account-access barriers, and any required calendar edit the assistant cannot perform. Name the service and exact step you must complete; keep the job pending. |
| **Ignore** | Marketing, duplicate notifications and messages without a scheduling task. Record the reason without contacting anyone. |

The scheduling policy must specify working hours, time zone, meeting lengths, buffers and commitments that cannot move. Missing preferences produce a draft or question, not invented availability.

While you are unreachable, the assistant may acknowledge, propose slots, chase a reply, reschedule or confirm **only to the extent explicitly covered by your send grant**. Each grant specifies known correspondents or a defined class of known correspondents, permitted intents, email as the channel, limits and expiry. A first-ever correspondent always requires your approval. Log the grant used for every send; allow immediate revocation. No blanket “send anything about scheduling” permission.

For example, you could authorize proposing available slots and one follow-up to established collaborators, while retaining approval for cancellations or displacing an existing meeting. That is a proposed policy, not an authorization already given. Without a matching grant, the assistant can draft while you are away but sends nothing—even a courtesy acknowledgment. An unanswered question remains on hold after its deadline; silence never selects the recommended option.

Agent-written emails identify their author plainly: “I’m an automated scheduling assistant acting for [your name].” Keep that disclosure on for unattended sends. You may omit it for a message you personally approve verbatim. Share only authorized scheduling information, not unrelated messages, calendar titles or reasons for unavailability.

Reach you through an authenticated, allow-listed owner channel configured at setup; email can serve initially, but phone alerts require an additional channel. Proposed defaults are two nonurgent notifications daily, quiet hours you select, and urgent interruptions only under agreed urgency rules. Use one thread per job, with its evidence, options and deadline. Failed delivery leaves the job pending. Share approvals and duplicate detection across channels; only your verified messages can change authority. Forwarded text and correspondents’ instructions cannot.

Keep a durable ledger containing the request, evidence, grant, next check and state: waiting-on-owner, waiting-on-third-party or done. Define completion per job: an email-send receipt proves sending, not a booked meeting. Mark scheduling complete only with the required counterpart confirmation and calendar evidence. After an interrupted send, inspect sent mail before retrying; an unknown outcome must not become a duplicate email.

responses.answer:
Use the full-duplex model for conversation and your own backend for coding work, connected asynchronously so a running command never blocks listening.

The voice layer owns listening, speaking, turn-taking, acknowledgements and interruption handling. It may understand the conversation, clarify scope, draft speech and relay requests or answers. Give it no file-write or shell-execution tools, secrets or authority to approve actions. A spoken ‘yes’ goes to the backend; the voice layer never executes it.

The backend owns planning, repository context, permissions, file edits, commands, verification and cancellation. Dispatch a bounded job only after its scope is clear, and track its identity and state independently of the audio session. The backend requests any necessary confirmation through the voice layer and checks that the reply covers the specific action. Treat transcripts as noisy: read back critical paths, identifiers and other exact values before an edit or command depends on them. Passwords and one-time codes belong in a secure user-controlled input, outside the voice relay.

If you interrupt mid-sentence, stop speaking and listen. The running command continues unless you explicitly request cancellation. Cancellation is a separate cooperative backend operation: stop admitting new steps, attempt to stop the active operation safely, and report what actually stopped or completed. It does not promise rollback. If interruption or reconnection loses the command’s result, mark its outcome unknown, recover its status and inspect the resulting state before acting again. Never automatically rerun a possibly completed command.

The backend sends either a progress note—what changed or what is blocking—or a terminal note containing the verified result, the limit that stopped work, or the one question requiring your input. The voice layer speaks the takeaway first, then the reason that matters, usually in a couple of sentences. It must distinguish ‘I plan to change this,’ ‘the command is running,’ and ‘the check passed.’ A spoken ‘done’ requires verification.

Keep exact commands, paths, diffs and error messages visible in the text interface; say that the details are there instead of reading raw logs aloud. If no visible surface exists, provide them in a text channel. Bound the voice session with a deadline and idle timeout; an explicit close ends the session and admits no further backend work, while already-started work retains its tracked status.

I’m applying Fabius’s media, consent and billing rules. I would not upload the photo or start a paid render yet.

1. **Resolve consent first.** Your marketing role and a public press photo do not establish permission to make the CEO appear to say a new line. I need documented permission covering her likeness, the line, intended use and any voice imitation. Without it, I decline the transfer and can draft a version with an invented, non-identifying presenter.

2. **Prepare the authorized request.** After consent, classify this as still-to-motion with lip-sync. Check the provider’s current schema for that capability, required speech input, five-second duration, highest-quality tier and source-image limits. Obtain the actual line and approved audio or voice choice; do not assume a photo supplies a voice. Review photo-use rights and hosted-service retention, training and deletion terms before uploading.

3. **Price before submitting.** Twenty five-second variations total 100 output-seconds. The rate is not supplied, so no monetary estimate is available. Read the exact tier’s current rate and billing conditions, show the total, and obtain a spending ceiling before the first paid job. I would propose a single preview before the batch; I would not silently lower your requested tier or change the count.

4. **Submit each approved variation once.** Persist an intent record with parameters, their hash and submission time before each request; save the returned job ID immediately. Because the API has no idempotency key, disable automatic submission retries. A 60-second timeout does not prove failure. With a job ID, resume polling that job. Without an ID, mark the outcome unknown and reconcile through a provider job list or usage view if available; otherwise require an account check. Never blindly resubmit and risk billing twice.

5. **Inspect and preserve the result.** Poll within a bounded budget; unfamiliar statuses are not success or failure. Preserve job IDs across timeouts. On confirmed success, inspect speech, lip-sync and duration, download and hash the file, and retain the prompt, parameters, model, job ID, source IDs, consent basis and terms date. Label published output synthetic and retain provenance marks.

I refuse to reword a blocked request or switch providers to evade moderation. I would report the block and offer a compliant revision; I would not claim a refund without provider confirmation.

The consent pause comes from [Fabius Custos §8](skills/fabius-praesidium/references/supply-chain-and-ai-artifacts.md): “No recorded consent basis → **decline the transfer step**”. The spending pause comes from [Pictor §4](skills/fabius-decor/references/generative-media.md): “none set → ask before the first paid submit.” Those rules apply because consent and a spending ceiling are both absent. No media has been uploaded and no paid job started.

The week-offline claim is not yet supported. Healthy containers establish process health; one warm-tab answer establishes only that that query worked in the current state. Neither proves cold startup, complete local dependencies or recovery. I’m applying Fabius’s offline-knowledge acceptance checks; this is a review and proposed plan, with nothing executed.

1. Define the promise. List required document questions, whether generated answers and maps are required, intended users and workload, acceptable response times, and maximum recovery time. Name the corpus edition and the seven-day period without updates.

2. Inventory while connected. Record document IDs, source/edition and retrieval dates, licences, local paths, hashes, scope and omissions. Inventory answer-model weights, tokenizer, embedding model and dimensions, runtime/container images, extraction/OCR dependencies and every first-run download or remote call. For maps, record required regions and zoom levels plus local tiles, styles and fonts. Uninventoried assets remain unverified.

3. Prove completeness and capacity. Reconcile expected documents against downloaded, readable, extracted and indexed IDs; expose failed, partial and browse-only sources. Inspect representative OCR, passages and tables. Bind indexes to source hashes and parser/chunker/model versions. On the actual 8 GB machine, measure peak RAM, disk headroom, CPU and accelerator availability under the promised workload; budget extraction, inference, index and update copies separately. Measure search and generation latency separately. Do not select a model from RAM alone. Direct reading or lexical search is an acceptable fallback only if it meets the agreed promise.

4. Test cold and disconnected. Within an authorized boundary, block external access while preserving required local networking, restart the appliance and use a fresh browser profile. Record attempted external requests and outcomes. Test an exact identifier, known passage, paraphrase and cross-document question; open every citation to the correct local page. Test missing/excluded sources, changed or removed documents, unavailable models and uncached map areas. Require honest unavailable answers, visible stale results or rejection of them, and explicit dependency failures. Display source dates; offline content must not appear newly refreshed.

5. Prove recovery separately. The PDF-only backup does not establish a recoverable appliance. Preserve originals, manifest and non-secret configuration, plus either a compatible index backup or a documented offline rebuild path. Preserve required model assets and other dependencies on recovery media. A missing vector index is tolerable only after rebuilding it offline succeeds. Restore into a fresh location without overwriting the working store or borrowing its caches; compare hashes, check links, repeat the disconnected probes and measure total recovery time.

6. Accept against recorded evidence. Retain the manifest, test commands, outputs, resource measurements and unresolved gaps. Exercise the expected seven-day operating cycle, including restarts and scheduled jobs; call shorter testing partial evidence. Accept only the capabilities that pass cold operation, workload and recovery criteria.

Keep the appliance labelled as source-grounded research retrieval. Citations support checking a document; they do not validate emergency decisions, diagnoses or treatment. Emergency and medical assistance need a separate workflow outside this acceptance claim.
